story: These mountains were thrust up by the collision of continents along the Alpine Fault, which the tracks cross in places between Sabine Hut and Lake Rotoiti. In the last Ice Age great glaciers gouged troughs in the headwaters of the Buller River; Lakes Rotoiti and Rotoroa, which give the park its name, now fill them. Ice, erosion and weathering have left steep valley sides, scree slopes, sharp arête ridges and many tarn-filled basins.

Beech rules the forest: red and silver beech on the valley floors, small-leaved mountain beech on the thinner soils above. In these honeydew beech forests a scale insect provides energy for nectar-feeding birds, and heavy seeding years feed seed-eaters. At the bushline the forest gives way to hebe, flax, dracophyllum and spiky spaniard, then tussock and alpine herbs. Kākā call from the forest, kea and rock wren visit the tops, whio ride the rapids, and great spotted kiwi have been brought back to the protected forest east of Lake Rotoiti.

Legend tells that Rakaihautu, chief and explorer, dug great holes with his ko, his digging stick, which filled with water, and stocked them with food for those who followed. The lakes, Rotoiti, 'little lake', and Rotoroa, 'long lake', with their eels, freshwater mussels and waterfowl, fed Māori travelling the pounamu trails to and from the West Coast. Māori guides such as Kehu led the early European explorers, among them Cotterell, Brunner, Heaphy, von Haast and Travers.

Grazing began in 1843 and spread over most of the ranges. Reserves were set around the two lakes in 1900, a national park was first proposed in 1906, and holiday cottages appeared at Rotoiti by 1925. The park was finally created in 1956, when the last grazing ended. In 1997 DOC made the forest around Lake Rotoiti one of six 'mainland islands', and pest control there has brought back a chorus of birdsong.
howItWorks: Nelson Lakes is run by the Department of Conservation (DOC) from the Nelson Lakes Visitor Centre in St Arnaud. Under the National Parks Act 1980 the public has freedom of entry and access, and there is no entry ticket; you pay for huts and campsites. The park's backcountry huts follow DOC's hut categories. Serviced huts, like most on the Travers–Sabine Circuit, have mattresses, water, toilets and heating, with seasonal fees on this circuit; standard huts are $15 an adult a night and basic huts free. Unbooked huts are paid with backcountry hut tickets, sold online from 1 November 2026, or a Backcountry Hut Pass ($140 for 12 months).

Angelus Hut, at 1,650 metres on the shore of Lake Angelus, and its campsite must be booked all year; no spaces are kept for walk-ins, and Backcountry Hut Passes are accepted there only from 1 May to 30 September. Kerr Bay campsite in St Arnaud is also booked all year. Water taxis run on both lakes, and many trampers start the Travers–Sabine Circuit with a boat to the head of Lake Rotoiti.

Dogs and other domestic animals are not allowed in the park; dogs kill kiwi. Mountain bikes are allowed only on formed roads. Rotomairewhenua/Blue Lake and Rotopōhueroa/Lake Constance are tapu to Ngāti Apa ki te Rā Tō: do not touch the water, swim, wash, take water or put any equipment in them. To stop the spread of lindavia, an invasive alga, clean wet gear at the stations at Coldwater, Lakehead and Sabine huts, and make sure gear is completely dry for 48 hours before using Lake Angelus or other alpine tarns.

sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-lake-rotoiti-and-ker: The glacial lake at St Arnaud, ringed by beech forest, with a campsite, boat ramp, lakeshore walks and the bird-filled Rotoiti Nature Recovery Project.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-lake-rotoroa: The 'long lake', reached by a side road between St Arnaud and Murchison; a water taxi links Rotoroa village with Sabine Hut.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-mount-robert: The peak above Lake Rotoiti; from Mount Robert car park the Pinchgut Track and the Robert Ridge route lead to Lake Angelus.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-rotomaninitua-lake-a: An alpine lake at 1,650 metres in the Travers Range, with Angelus Hut on its shore. Frozen in most winters, May to October.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-whisky-falls: A waterfall a short diversion off the Lakeside Track on the western shore of Lake Rotoiti, on the way to Coldwater Hut.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-travers-falls: A 20-metre cascade plunging into a deep bowl, a short side track above John Tait Hut on the Travers–Sabine Circuit.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-poukirikiri-travers-: The circuit's alpine pass, 450 metres above Upper Travers Hut, with panoramic views and a steep 1,000-metre descent to the Sabine forks. Freezing conditions possible all year.
sightNotes.poi-nz-nelson-lakes-rotomairewhenua-blue: Thought to be the clearest natural freshwater lake in the world, an overnight side trip up the West Sabine. Tapu: do not touch the water.

planYourVisit.reservations: Angelus Hut and its campsite, and Kerr Bay campsite, must be booked all year; Angelus bookings are open for stays to 30 June 2027. Other huts are covered by hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass. Water taxis on both lakes are booked with the operators.

Weddings in the park: contact the Nelson Lakes Visitor Centre

Lake Rotoroa campsite, and a booked campsite beside Angelus Hut

chronology.text: Cotterell, guided by Māori, visits the lakes; the area has drawn visitors ever since.
Grazing begins; the first run at Lake Rotoiti is established in 1848.
The first reserves are set aside around Lakes Rotoiti and Rotoroa.
A national park is first proposed.
Nelson Lakes National Park is created, and grazing in the ranges ends.
An avalanche destroys forest in the West Sabine valley, below Blue Lake.
The Rotoiti Nature Recovery Project begins as one of DOC's six mainland islands.

safety: If you doubt your abilities or the weather, particularly near Poukirikiri/Travers Saddle or at unbridged streams after heavy rain, turn back.

Avalanches threaten the alpine routes and some huts in winter and spring. John Tait Hut lies below an avalanche path: do not use it in storms or when snow reaches the valley floor. Read DOC's avalanche information for the park before you go.

All routes to Lake Angelus are alpine, and the Mount Cedric route is very exposed; from May to October they carry snow, ice and avalanche risk, and winter trips need ice axe, crampons and navigation skills.
DOC strongly recommends carrying a personal locator beacon. Carry antihistamine if you react to wasp stings.
Follow the Land Safety Code from DOC and the NZ Mountain Safety Council: choose the right trip, understand the weather, pack warm clothes and extra food, share your plans, and fill in the hut book.
regulations: No dogs or other domestic animals in the park.
Mountain bikes only on formed roads.
Do not touch, swim in, wash in or take water from Rotomairewhenua/Blue Lake or Rotopōhueroa/Lake Constance.
Clean wet gear at the lindavia stations and dry it for 48 hours before entering Lake Angelus or other alpine tarns.
No fires at Kerr Bay campsite at any time; keep to the tracks, away from pest-control toxins and traps.

weather: Freezing conditions and heavy rain can come at any time of year, and Poukirikiri/Travers Saddle can freeze in any month. For the Travers–Sabine Circuit the weather and snow are most favourable from October to May, though in some years snow lingers on the alpine passes into late November. In most years Lake Angelus freezes and snow blankets the routes to it from May to October, when you may have to dig your way to the hut; winter trips need ice axe, crampons, goggles and avalanche awareness. After heavy rain some unbridged streams are unsafe to cross. Wasps are numerous from January to April.
directions: St Arnaud is about an hour and a half by road from Nelson or Blenheim. State Highway 63 from Blenheim reaches St Arnaud and Lake Rotoiti; a side road about halfway between St Arnaud and Murchison leads to Lake Rotoroa. Buses to St Arnaud run only irregularly, so ask the Nelson Lakes Visitor Centre, and several companies offer on-demand transport from St Arnaud and Nelson to Rotoroa. Water taxis run on both lakes. Isolated car parks are prone to theft: leave nothing valuable in your car, and use the bag storage at the visitor centre.
